item.title: John Thune Isn’t Bowing to Trump’s Pressure: ‘Show Me How This Ends’
item.description: A standoff over the restrictive voting bill Trump is pushing has left nerves raw at the Capitol, with even the typically staid Thune showing signs of frustration.

media:content.media:description: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) speaks following a policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 21, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
There’s an inherent tension between any President and the Senate Majority Leader. George W. Bush and his team did everything they could in 2004 to make Tom Daschle the first party leader in the Senate to lose re-election since 1952. Barack Obama, who hired Daschle’s top aide as his own when he won a seat in the the Senate that same year, had a respectful but strained relationship with Harry Reid, who praised him as a "light-skinned African-American" with "no Negro dialect, unless he wanted to have one.” Donald Trump insulted Mitch McConnell as “Old Crow.” And Chuck Schumer drove out to Joe Biden’s beach house in Delaware after a calamitous debate performance against Trump to tell his former Senate colleague that he had to end his re-election bid for the good of the party. 

Trump’s dynamic with his current counterpart John Thune is now rapidly climbing that pressure scale. 

“That’s too bad for him and too bad for the Republican Party. He’s got the votes. He should get it done,” Trump told reporters of Thune in the Oval Office on Wednesday when asked about a restrictive voting measure that is, at least for now, D.O.A. in the upper chamber.

It was mild ding by Trump’s standards, for sure. But it speaks to the frayed relationship between the two Republicans, who are in a standoff over Trump’s latest fixation, a bill that would remake how Americans vote. Thune has been clear that the proposed legislation, which has cleared the House, lacks the votes it needs in the Senate and there is no appetite for changing the rules to ease its passage. Put plainly: Thune knows the headcount and isn’t wasting the time on something that is doomed, and Trump does not much care for that.

"If I thought there was a path to getting a result, I'm all for it," Thune told reporters this week.

The Senate is racing toward an August recess with a packed to-do list that seems doable: a sanctions bill targeting Russia, a stopgap funding measure to keep the government open through Election Day, movement on a catch-all reconciliation bill, and a bunch of nominees, including one that on Wednesday seemed to inch closer to giving Trump an up-or-down on his imperiled pick for Attorney General. But Trump says the upper chamber should not leave town until it gives him the SAVE America Act, his voting bill. He also wants the Senate to change its threshold for moving most legislation from 60 votes to 51 votes, ending the delay machine of the filibuster. 

“John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to ‘leave town’ until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER, where Republicans can then quickly pass everything they ever dreamed of, including a full and deep throated SAVE AMERICA ACT, the Budget, and the ever looming Debt Ceiling disaster, 1929!” the President wrote on his social media platform. “The Dumocrats will do it on day one, and can’t believe how lucky they got with this Senate leadership.”

In response to which Thune had a polite brush-off. 

“If the endgame is, we actually get an outcome or result, we could stay here until Christmas,” Thune said. “But Democrats aren’t voting for this, I’m just telling you. And the Republicans are not getting rid of the legislative filibuster.”

The situation has left nerves raw at the Capitol, with the typically staid Thune showing signs of frustration. "Show me how this ends. What's the picture of victory at the end?" Thune said.

The White House has already summoned close to two dozen Republican Senators to pressure them directly to end the filibuster. According to a senior Republican aide on the Hill, 15 of the 20 who took the meetings told the White House staff directly that they were a hard no on the shift when it comes to the sacrosanct tool of obstruction.

“This is not an open question. It’s just a fact, and the facts don’t change,” Thune said.

That doesn’t mean the White House accepts it. Last week, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt ominously told reporters that Trump’s “patience is running out” when it comes to the Senate passing the SAVE America Act.

But that fuse has flames racing from both ends. 

Unlike House Speaker Mike Johnson, the GOP in the Senate is largely of the same mind that Trumpism will ultimately be only an era. Also, unlike the election to pick the chief of the House, Senate leadership elections are conducted by private ballot, so there’s less risk of running afoul of Trump’s whims. And added to that, Senators are elected to six-year terms, meaning they have a little more padding against any one vote.

It’s also just seen as bad politics in an environment that could give Democrats the Senate majority if the GOP base stays home. “Disappointing [the President] but also our voters 99 days before the election strikes me as a bad idea,” said Sen. John Cornyn, a Texas Republican who once was a contender for Thune’s role and lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed candidate.

As a result, Senate Republicans are more hardened against Trump’s pressure than their House colleagues—and the understood reality is that Thune himself is nowhere near risk, even as the current storm between the Senate Majority leader and the President builds.

Cornyn was blunt in his assessment of the situation: the Senate “can stay here ‘til the cows come home, and it’s not going to change anything.”

The conservative Senate Republican Conference has been circulating a memo to members telling them that staying in Washington for August would make sense if it could move the needle—but it won’t.

“I don’t think staying in session will make more votes appear. … And we have work to do at home to make sure that we beat the Democrats in November,” the memo advises lawmakers to say. 

That said, Trump has gotten some lawmakers on side in publicly backing his desire for the upper chamber to spend a sticky August casting votes for legislation that would likely not make much of a difference in this year’s midterms in any case. They include Mike Lee of Utah, Rick Scott and Ashley Moody of Florida, Tommy Tuberville of Alabama, Jim Banks of Indiana, Darlene Graham of South Carolina and Bill Hagerty of Tennessee—all red-state Republicans whose seats are generally seen as safe holds.

But even if the Senate were to stay in town, the math is not mathing. “We simply don’t have the votes,” Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota said. 

That doesn’t mean Trump will stop pushing for them.

item.title: What Is a Fire Cloud and How Are They Making Europe's Wildfires More Dangerous?
item.description: As firefighters in France and Spain battle to get the blazes under control, an expert breaks down the ​phenomenon of fire clouds for TIME.

media:content.media:description: The beach of Moutchic in Lacanau, southwestern France, as clouds of smoke rise into the sky from the Gironde wildfire on July 24, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Ferocious wildfires in France and Spain have prompted the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people, as firefighters battle against changing winds to keep the blazes under control.

An added difficulty has developed in France thanks to the emergence of a rare meteorological phenomenon—a pyrocumulonimbus, more commonly known as a "fire cloud." 

Officials in the badly-impacted Gironde region, near Bordeaux, confirmed the formation of what is understood to be France’s first-ever reported fire cloud over the weekend.

As of Wednesday afternoon, firefighters in the south-western Gironde region continued battling the blazes as temperatures reached around 39°C (near 102°F) amid another western Europe heat wave.

Satellite imagery of Castellón, a province near Valencia, Spain, also shows what is thought to be a "towering pyrocumulus" fire cloud rising above part of the impacted area.

Amid concern the high temperatures may result in the fires worsening or contained blazes restarting, there are also fears that fire clouds, often thought of as fire-generated thunderstorms, could make the wildfires more dangerous.

Sophie Brocas, the prefect of Gironde, told reporters the firestorms created by the phenomenon were a sign the crisis had entered a “new dimension.”

Here’s what you need to know about the rare ​phenomenon—and the hazards associated with it.

What is a fire cloud?

Described by NASA as a "fire-breathing dragon of clouds," fire clouds are created by the intense heat of wildfires, generating an updraft of superheated, fast-rising air that can trigger powerful storms.

Jean-Baptiste Filippi, a researcher at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), tells TIME that the clouds fall into two categories: pyrocumulus and pyrocumulonimbus (also known as pyroCb).

He explains that pyrocumulus is the first stage of a fire cloud. As the wildfire releases large amounts of heat, the air near the ground heats up and rises rapidly, generating a strong upward current.

"That's level one, because you're adding this to the energy of the fire to create the convective column," he says, referring to a vertical stream of hot, rising gas.

As the warm air reaches higher layers of the atmosphere, it cools and expands. When the temperature falls low enough, the water vapor in the air begins to condense, forming a cloud above the smoke column.

"Level two is pyrocumulonimbus," he says. "Imagine now that this energy is enough to overshoot the lower atmosphere and go up to almost the stratosphere."

For this process to occur, there needs to be a combination of intense heat from the wildfire and extreme weather conditions that allow the cloud to develop.

"The energy is there anyway. It's ready to be released," Filippi says. "It's going to be triggered on top of the fire, and then it will start to interact and make it blow up. If the fire was not there, it would probably be a storm, but somewhere else."

It is the combination of weather conditions that would ordinarily produce a dry thunderstorm and an active wildfire that creates this phenomenon.

"It's because both are occurring at the same time, and it's this combo that is causing the problem," Filippi tells TIME.

How do fire clouds make wildfires more dangerous?

Fire clouds can make areas already engulfed by wildfire significantly more hazardous—not only for firefighters trying to contain the blaze, but also for people living nearby.

The clouds create conditions that can make fires stronger and allow them to spread more rapidly.

Filippi explains that the storms created by the pyrocumulonimbus, which loom over the fire, create gusts of wind, which in turn lead the water vapor further into the clouds.

"Then the fire is raging more and propagating at [a] higher speed with more energy, so it injects even more water vapor. The cloud is getting bigger, and then it is sucking air [in a stronger way]. Then you have this feedback loop, making an acceleration," Filippi says.

Those conditions make fires more difficult to contain because the feedback loop continually strengthens both the fire and the cloud above it.

Additionally, studies have found wildfire smoke can make some clouds denser, making it harder for them to drop rain that could help dampen the fires.

Even when water droplets do fall, if the rain is falling into hot air, "it's gonna evaporate before it reaches the ground," Filippi says.

Instead, "you're gonna have a big downdraft. You're gonna have thunder. Then you can have some other effects, like lifting ashes up into the stratosphere," he notes, adding that the ash could later fall onto neighboring areas, raising the need for precautionary evacuation measures.

"It's also lifting burning material, like spotting fire, so it does propagate some burning pieces of wood that could fall down afterwards," he says.

Fire clouds are expected to become more common

Pyrocumulus and pyrocumulonimbus remain relatively rare in Europe. Further afield, fire clouds were observed during Australia's 2019-20 bushfires and in California's 2020 wildfire season.

Filippi warns, however, that climate change could make these events more common in Europe.

"You need stormy conditions, and then you need fire. We are going to have more stormy conditions, and we are going to have more fire. So the probability of having both together, at the same place and at the same time, is higher," he says.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has referred to the current wildfire crisis as "the most painful expression" of the climate emergency.

"You have more energy in the atmosphere with climate change, you have more water vapor in the atmosphere because the sun is evaporating more water from the oceans," Filippi says. "So more water and vapor means more latent energy. That is just one thing to be released. That's why you have more rain too, and more floods, so the potential of storms is higher."

As such, governments have already started preparing for more extreme weather conditions.

In France, the government earlier this year launched an initiative to expand mandatory vegetation-clearance rules in an effort to reduce the intensity and spread of fires around buildings.

Spain introduced a new national Forest Fire Danger Index at the start of the summer, which combined weather data with satellite observations of vegetation, soil moisture, and land use, allowing authorities to identify areas of extreme danger of forest fires.

Signifying the growing concern across western Europe, the U.K. government also strengthened its wildfire resilience heading into the warmer months.

item.title: Breaking Down the Surprisingly Emotional Ending of Shark Thriller The Devil’s Mouth
item.description: A group of friends take a tour through a remote cave system, only to get trapped with a deadly shark

media:content.media:description: Kathryn Newton and Lana Condor in The Devil's Mouth

item.content:encoded:
Warning: This post contains spoilers for The Devil’s Mouth.

Prime Video’s The Devil's Mouth begins with a carefree vacation between a group of lifelong friends in Thailand. Sara (Kathryn Newton), Max (Lana Condor), James (Nico Hiraga), Greg (Gavin Casalegno), and Adrienne (Tommi Rose) set out on one last adventure before their lives take different paths, joining a guided tour through a remote cave system known as the Devil's Mouth.

However, their trip takes a terrifying turn after water from a recent storm floods the caves with sea life, leaving the group trapped with a deadly bull shark. As panic spreads and their chances of escape grow slimmer, long-buried tensions begin to fracture their friendships.

As the group fights to survive, Sara is forced to confront her fears, step into a leadership role, and discover a strength she never believed she had—changing the dynamic of her friendship with Max, who has always been the more confident and assertive one.

Despite the killer shark, director Jeff Wadlow says the emotional core of the film is the relationship between Sara and Max.

"I was told it's a shark movie in a cave... and I was like, well, I'm in," Wadlow says. "But then I read the script, and there was this really nuanced, complex female friendship at its core. That made me want to make the movie even more."

Here's what happens at the end of The Devil's Mouth.

What is the Devil's Mouth?

In The Devil's Mouth, the Devil's Mouth is a remote freshwater cave system in Thailand. While on vacation, Sara, Max, and their friends join a guided tour through its interconnected caverns, flooded chambers, and narrow rocky passages. After arriving at the cave entrance by kayak, they continue the excursion by swimming through the cave system.

Before entering the caves, the group's guide, Wat (Tayme Thapthimthong), explains that there are two possible routes. The green path is the standard tour and considered the safer option, while the red path is longer, more challenging, and riskier. He also warns that a recent storm triggered an early monsoon surge, making parts of the cave system more dangerous than usual.

Despite the warning, Max persuades both the guide and the rest of the group to choose the red path instead. The guide reluctantly agrees, a decision that ultimately leaves the friends trapped deep inside the cave system and sets the film's events in motion.


Why is there a shark in the cave?

The shark enters the Devil's Mouth cave system through an opening in the cave wall that connects to the ocean. Under normal conditions, the caves are a freshwater environment, but the storm surge and high tide push seawater further into the system than usual.

These unusual conditions explain why Sara discovers an ominous dead saltwater fish inside the caves before the group encounters a much larger ocean creature.

They discover it’s a bull shark, a species capable of living in both saltwater and freshwater. This adaptation allows the shark to remain inside the cave system and hunt the group as they struggle to find a way out.

Who dies in The Devil's Mouth?


The danger inside the Devil's Mouth cave system becomes clear when Ryan (Harrison Luna), the diver who spoke with Sara before the group entered the caves, is attacked by the shark. After Sara discovers blood in the water and his damaged diving mask, the group realizes that they are trapped with a predator inside the cave. As the group tries to find a way out, Wat attempts to escape after the shark is discovered. However, the friends later hear his scream and realize that he did not survive.


The shark continues to threaten the group as they attempt to escape through the flooded passages. Greg becomes the first of Sara's friends to die when the shark attacks him in the water. Shortly after, Adrianne falls back into the water from the ledge where the group had stopped. Sara, Max, and James try to pull her back up, but the shark reaches her first.


James later becomes trapped while the group is moving through the narrow underwater tunnels. A rock collapse blocks his way, and although Sara and Max try to free him, they cannot get him out. James eventually drowns, leaving Sara and Max to continue alone.


Max is the film's final victim. After Sara finds a possible way out of the cave, the two friends attempt to climb toward the opening. Sara helps Max, who is struggling because of her injured hand, but the shark leaps out of the water and pulls Max back.

According to Wadlow, Max's emotional exchange with Sara before the shark attacks was added just days before filming began. He felt the scene was essential to showing that Max finally acknowledged Sara's growth. "We wanted to understand that not only had Sara grown and changed, but that Max recognized it," he says.

Condor explains that Max begins the film as someone who believes she always knows best. "She feels that she is the leader," Condor says. "She's incredibly headstrong, disrespectful, annoying." However, the cave forces Max to confront the consequences of her confidence and the limits of her own judgment. "She realizes that she doesn't know everything. And she's not right about everything," Condor adds.



How does Sara survive?

Before Max's death, Sara and Max discover an opening that could lead outside the cave. However, they realize the drop is too high to escape safely. Their plan is to wait for the tide to rise, allowing them to jump safely into the ocean from the opening without risking a dangerous fall.

After Max dies, Sara is alone inside the cave. She uses the flare she was carrying to distract the shark and force it away. With it still following her, Sara creates a trap using the unstable rocks inside the cave. She draws the shark toward her and causes it to repeatedly crash into the rocks, until they eventually collapse and crush the shark.

After defeating the shark, Sara searches for another way out of the cave. She finds a second opening in the cave system and climbs through it, emerging near the beach, with trees and sand surrounding the area. Unlike the previous opening that led out toward the ocean, this exit allows Sara to reach land and finally escape the Devil's Mouth alive.

Reflecting on Sara's transformation, Newton says portraying her growth required embracing the character's initial insecurity and her reliance on Max as a source of confidence. "I didn't like that Sara was such a baby and had to lean into it to discover her strength," she says. She also highlights the importance of Sara and Max's complicated friendship, explaining that Wadlow was drawn to "how they have to really turn against each other to find each other."

By the end of the film, Sara becomes the one making the decisions and taking control of her own survival. "Once I became the apex predator that a teenage girl is, I couldn't be stopped," Newton adds.

What does the ending mean?

Although Sara survives the Devil's Mouth, the ending leaves her carrying the weight of everything she lost inside the cave. For Newton, the final scene is less about victory and more about the reality of growing up and facing life on your own.

"I love the end of the movie. I think it's like a really extreme allegory for youth and coming of age," Newton says. "You have to be alone and be okay with it. You have to love yourself and then love everyone else and appreciate people while you have them."

For Condor, the ending also represents the moment when Max is forced to confront how she has always viewed Sara. She explains that their friendship is built on years of history, but Max has always seen Sara as someone who would follow her lead rather than as an equal.

"Max fully believes that she's always gonna have Sara in her back pocket as like her sidekick," Condor says. "But I don't think she considers Sara an individual at all."

Condor says Max's final moments are meaningful because they give her a chance to acknowledge her own mistakes and realize that she never truly saw Sara as her own person. "Being able to admit that you're wrong, or admit that you haven't always been the best friend or the best support to the people around you... I think that's really beautiful," she says. "It's never too late to tell someone, 'Hey, listen, I was wrong. And I see you.'"

item.title: The True Story Behind Netflix's The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare
item.description: As Bryan Kohberger challenges his conviction for murdering four Idaho college students, a new Netflix documentary examines what we know about the case

media:content.media:description: From left, University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in a November 2022 attack at an off-campus house in Moscow.

item.content:encoded:
In July 2025, a judge sentenced criminology graduate student Bryan Kohberger to life in prison after he pleaded guilty to stabbing four college students to death on Nov. 13, 2022, at a house near the University of Idaho’s Moscow, Id., campus. The students were Ethan Chapin, 20, Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Madison Mogen, 21. 

A year later, Kohberger told the New York Times in a phone call from prison that he’s filed a petition challenging his conviction, arguing that he is innocent and did not mean to confess to the killings. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions,” he told the Times from a maximum security prison south of Boise. “I really do want that to be heard.”

The comments from Kohberger came days before a new documentary about the case premiered on Netflix. The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare, out July 29, traces how police found Kohberger’s DNA on a knife sheath left behind at the crime scene, identified his getaway car, and figured out that his cell phone went off-grid around the time he committed the crime. The three-part series features interviews with families and friends of the victims, people who knew Kohberger, and law enforcement officials to examine what we know about the case.

The mystery of the motive

Because Kohberger pleaded guilty a month before he was scheduled to stand trial, it remains unclear why he targeted these four college students.

“Ultimately we never have been able to answer that question that everybody wants answered: ‘Why?’” says Moscow Police Chief Anthony Dahlinger. “We don’t know, ‘Why these four?’ We don’t know, ‘Why this house?’ I don’t think we’ll ever know.”

The documentary's participants suggest that Kohberger may have been studying criminology so he could carry out the perfect crime. The series features Lilly Karaban, who sat next to Kohberger in an undergraduate criminology class on serial killers at DeSales University and said he dominated class discussions and wouldn’t let her get a word in on a group project. She says she didn’t see him socializing outside of class, describing him as being “in his own world.”

Kohberger was doing a PhD in criminology at Washington State University, a 10-minute drive from the University of Idaho, and several female students told authorities that he was unpleasant to be around. In one instance, a female student said he followed her to her car and spoke to her in an aggressive manner, making her feel uncomfortable. The series also highlights a questionnaire that Kohberger posted on Reddit as part of a supposed research project, asking people who had been incarcerated how they chose and approached victims.

In the aftermath of the murders, Karaban says she believes Kohberger “has a thing against women, based on the description of what he did to those three poor girls. People who brutalize women the way Kohberger did dislike them, find them threatening. So they take all that anger out on them.”

Trying to find closure

Families interviewed in the documentary have mixed feelings about the plea deal and had been anticipating a trial. 

As director Skye Borgman says, “If there had been some ask of the perpetrator to—in exchange for this plea deal—give some information as to the why, I think it would have helped the families a lot. They’re angry.”  

Some of the victims’ families are disappointed that he didn’t receive the death penalty, feeling like he got off easy. Kaylee Goncalves’ dad Steve dismissed prison as “daycare.” His daughter Alivea says she felt “hurt” by the plea deal and didn’t think it should have been an option for Kohberger, arguing, “Monsters like that should never-ever ever have options ever again.” 

Moscow Police’s Dahlinger maintains that, in a way, Kohberger received a form of the death penalty: “He is sentenced to die in prison.” 

Xana’s dad Jeff Kernodle says the victims’ families were hoping to hear more from Kohberger, arguing, “He should have to tell them why he did it, tell all of us parents why he did it.” 

On the other hand, Xana’s sister Jazzmin Kernodle says in the series she was dreading a trial that could last months. “I think the plea deal did save us a lot of emotional trauma that we would have dealt with going through a trial,” she says. “I am grateful to get it over with and slowly start to heal.”

item.title: Could Wildfires Overshadow Spain’s Solar Eclipse?
item.description: Spain is in the path of totality for a solar eclipse next week—the mainland’s first since 1905. But will wildfire smoke and mass evacuations disrupt the highly anticipated experience?

media:content.media:description: Fire engines stop on a road as smoke rises from a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, on July 26, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Spain will be in the path of totality for a solar eclipse on Aug. 12. Not only is it the first time this type of celestial event has been visible to the mainland since 1905—it is also taking place during Europe’s peak tourism season, which runs from June to August. Millions of people live within the 190-mile-wide eclipse path, which reaches 36 of the nation’s 50 provinces, while hundreds of thousands of international travelers are also expected to visit for the occasion. 

Tourists are expected to flock to cities and towns along the path of totality—including parts of Aragón, Castilla y León, Castilla-La Mancha, and Valencia—as well as nearby hubs, where a deep partial eclipse will be visible, like the capital city of Madrid. 

But with multiple wildfires raging amid a particularly hot and dry summer, the rare experience of observing a total solar eclipse may be disrupted by evacuations and widespread smoke.

Read More: What to Know About the Deadly Wildfires in Western Europe

What are the fire conditions leading up to the eclipse?

While Spain is used to wildfires, record-breaking heat in June created a tinderbox in Western Europe, prompting two catastrophic fires: one that broke out on July 24, in the Guadalajara province just northeast of Madrid, devastating over 32,000 hectares (79,000 acres), and another in Ávila, which is in central Spain, that has burned more than 50,000 hectares (123,500 acres) since July 22. The Ávila fire is now the “largest forest fire in our country’s recent history” according to a statement on Sunday from the minister of ecological transition, Sara Aageson.

Together with numerous other fires across the country, they put Spain on track for its worst wildfire season in over three decades. Over 150,000 hectares (370,600 acres) have burned since January, according to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez—which is six times the area destroyed during the same period last year. Prior to 2025, the worst wildfire year for the country was 1994.

Sánchez said over the weekend that the “scale of the disaster we are living through is very hard to accept.” More than 90,000 tourists and residents have been evacuated or placed under shelter at home orders across central Spain, in parts of Madrid, Toledo, and Ávila. Spanish authorities said at least two people were killed in the eastern provinces of Castellón and Valencia

Sánchez also expressed concern about the weather conditions this week, which brings peak temperatures of nearly 40°C (104°F). Extreme heat makes it difficult to fight existing fires and adds the threat of new ones, which would challenge Spain’s already-stretched resources. 

With additional factors such as gusting winds and a lack of recent rainfall, the fire danger conditions in the country have been classified as “very extreme,” according to the European Forest Fires Information System (EFFIS). 

And those conditions are not likely to improve ahead of the solar eclipse, according to Jason Nicholls, senior meteorologist at AccuWeather.

“There's a heat wave going on right now, which carries into the weekend,” he tells TIME. “It may ease back a little bit, but then tries to come back again as we get into the week of August 10.”

“I don't see a lot of significant rain coming into Spain over the next two weeks, so drought conditions will continue to not improve, or even worsen,” he continues, explaining that “wildfire risk will remain extreme across a whole lot of Spain” in the days leading up to the solar eclipse.

How the wildfires could impact eclipse viewers

The wildfires will likely affect both visibility and air quality for eclipse viewers in the country, Becky Wagner, air quality and climate researcher at the University of Sheffield, tells TIME. 

The smoke from the fires contains  “particulate matter” consisting of burnt material, she explains.

“Firstly, that can affect visibility because these particles can reflect the sunlight and just create a haze and a sort of a cloud that is really hard to see through,” Wagner says.

But there is also the question of air quality, which could hinder viewers’ ability to safely stand outside and observe the eclipse. 

“There's high levels of this smoke, and high levels of the particulate matter within the smoke, which is really harmful to human health, as these particles are really small,” Wagner says, referring to a type of fine air pollutant known as PM2.5, which has been linked to lung cancer and heart disease. “They can be breathed in, and it can affect people's health, particularly vulnerable populations with respiratory and cardiovascular problems.”

Totality occurs when the moon passes exactly between the sun and the Earth, blocking out the daylight and casting impacted areas into complete darkness for about three minutes. While the experience of totality is brief, breathing in wildfire smoke can make people sick “right away,” leading to coughing and headaches, among other symptoms, according to the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 

And many eclipse-chasers will seek to observe the phenomenon beyond the moments of totality. Observation often begins as soon as the moon is visible in front of the sun, and lasts until it has completely passed by, meaning that the complete experience of a solar eclipse can span some two to three hours. 

But it’s hard to predict how current conditions might impact the air quality in mid-August, Wagner says, especially as wildfires can often create their own mini weather conditions. 

Particles “can last in the atmosphere for days to weeks, and they can be transported a really long distance, depending on sort of wind direction and wind speed,” Wagner says. 

Aside from Spain’s progress in quelling the fires this week, there are still active fires in France to consider, since the particulate matter could continue drifting across large portions of its neighboring nation. Wagner points to the wildfires in Canada earlier this month that drifted thousands of miles into the United States, worsening air quality in cities from Detroit to Manhattan.

“So fires in one region of Spain, or one region of Europe, could end up affecting different parts of the country or different countries,” she explains.

Still, Nicholls says that residents in Spain should be able to experience and enjoy the eclipse—with the proper precautions. He recommends wearing a mask when outdoors to avoid inhaling dangerous smoke, as well as limiting exposure to it.

“Maybe hang around inside, and as you get closer to the eclipse, maybe come outside and maybe have a mask on,” he recommends. Then “get back inside to get away from the harmful smoke and poor air quality.”

Read More: Photos Show the Destruction in France and Spain From Ferocious European Wildfires

What are the potential economic repercussions for Spain?

Access to viewing locations could also be impacted by the fires. One of the larger outbreaks is near Valencia—Spain’s third-largest city, which is situated along the Mediterranean. Last month, Space.com said that its beaches will be one of the easiest places to catch a glimpse of the eclipse. But local wildfires could potentially inhibit access to the beaches and other prime viewing spots. Such restrictions could be especially detrimental in light of the surge of tourists Spain is expecting next week—and might even have economic repercussions.

According to Spain’s Ministry of Tourism, the country continues to see an increase in international travelers year over year. And, despite the fires, the ministry is expecting a larger-than-usual boost in tourism next month, with dedicated umbraphiles—or eclipse chasers—traveling just for the occasion. 

“Between August 10 and 16, Spain will welcome 446,000 additional visitors due to the total solar eclipse,” the government said in a statement to TIME, citing an economic impact report from the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Business. “A 7.9% increase in scheduled airline seats is projected, compared to the same period in 2025, as well as a 17.8% rise in hotel reservations for August, compared to the same month last year.”

“It is clear that this event will have a very positive impact on our economy,” the Ministry of Tourism wrote, saying that it is expected to bring in 347.5 million euros ($395 million). The government has not revised its projections due to the wildfires; however, it says that the consequences to tourism are not its primary focus.

“The priority is to address the emergency posed by these fires, protect human lives, preserve the natural surroundings, and minimize the impact on the environment,” the statement said.

But the government’s statement also acknowledged that it has “a Special Security Plan and a Specific Civil Protection Plan” in place for the eclipse, which addresses wildfire prevention in particular, as well as increasing the response capacity of public services in preparations for the large gatherings that are anticipated for the special event.

Spain has yet to issue any travel advisories in response to the fires, but the United Kingdom last week began warning its residents—who make up nearly 20% of annual travelers to Spain—to take precautions if traveling through affected areas of Madrid and Ávila.

item.title: How to Help the Victims of Europe’s Deadly Wildfires
item.description: The devastating blazes have impelled what are believed to be France and Spain's largest peacetime evacuation operations in modern history, displacing roughly 330,000 people.
item.content:encoded:
Huge wildfires have torn through France and Spain, leaving several people dead and displacing hundreds of thousands of others.

The devastating blazes have shattered records for the largest wildfires on record in both countries and impelled what are believed to be the largest peacetime evacuation operations France and Spain have conducted in modern history, driving roughly 330,000 people from their homes and vacation sites.

Officials have estimated that more than 400,000 acres have burned in Spain this year and another 300,000 in France amid a series of blistering European heat waves. 

Read More: What to Know About the Deadly Wildfires in Western Europe

Firefighters succeeded in containing some of the major blazes in the two countries by Wednesday morning, but with temperatures once again expected to spike this week, authorities cautioned that the battle was not yet over and continued to evacuate thousands of people in threatened regions.

The European Union’s emergency response center meanwhile warned that still more countries will confront a heightened wildfire risk in the coming weeks.

"The next risk, it's already moving to Greece and also Central Europe," Maria Zuber, head of the European Union Emergency Response Coordination Center, told reporters on Wednesday.

"Greece for the moment was spared, and now we see that it will go to Greece. Italy will face risk at the beginning of August, and we will need to see what will happen with the Iberian Peninsula, because if [it is] there as well, we will have all Europe on fire," she said.

Here are ways you can help the victims impacted by the wildfires.

Red Cross

The International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies has mobilized relief efforts in both Spain and France, where teams from the national Red Cross organizations are providing emergency shelter, food, water, medical care, and other essential supplies and support to thousands of displaced people.

Cruz Roja, the Spanish Red Cross, is collecting donations here to support its ongoing wildfire response. 

You can also donate to local branches of the Croix-Rouge Francaise, the French Red Cross, that are working on the front lines of the fires in the southwestern part of the country here and here.

World Central Kitchen

World Central Kitchen, the hunger-fighting nonprofit organization founded by celebrity chef and TIME100 Philanthropy honoree José Andrés, is working to provide meals to people in need in both Spain and France in response to the wildfires.

You can donate to its efforts in Ávila‎, Spain, here and those in Bordeaux, France, here. 

Secours Populaire Français

Secours Populaire Français, a French nonprofit dedicated to combating poverty, is soliciting volunteers and donations to support the people severely affected by the wildfires in Gironde, Landes, and everywhere else in the country where the blazes are raging.

“The immediate crisis is real, but it will also be a long-term challenge,” the organization wrote. “Once the fires are extinguished, families will still need help rebuilding their lives and navigating the necessary procedures, isolated individuals will need support, and local businesses will need to resume their activities.”

You can make a donation here.

Sud Ouest Solidarité

Sud Ouest Solidarité, the charitable arm of one of France’s largest regional newspapers, has launched a fundraising campaign to collect donations for people affected by the fires and the firefighters working to combat them.

The organization said in a Tuesday post on its social media accounts that nearly 500,000 euros had so far been raised through the campaign.

You can donate here.

item.title: The Lone Republican Who Voted Against Advancing Bill to Put Tougher Sanctions on Russia
item.description: The lawmaker referred to the legislation as the "latest counterproductive attempt to hold Russia accountable for its war against Ukraine."

media:content.media:description: Republican Senators Ron Johnson of Wisconsin and Rand Paul of Kentucky are seated during a hearing in Washington, D.C. on July 29, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The Senate opted to advance a sweeping Russia sanctions bill backed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, but amid the bipartisan support there was one notable “nay” from a GOP lawmaker.

Named in honor of Graham, who died unexpectedly earlier this month, the bill advanced by a 86-12 vote late Tuesday, with Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky the only Republican to vote against it. 

Paul, who has previously raised issues with former versions of the bill, argued the legislation is the “latest counterproductive attempt to hold Russia accountable for its war against Ukraine, now well into its fifth year.”

“This legislation is a tariff bill that seems to have been written with such blind rage that, rather than compel a change in Vladimir Putin’s behavior, its punitive measures would make American families poorer and undermine our national interests,” he said last week, in an opinion piece for Fox News.

Some of Paul’s concerns regarding the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” were shared by others, with Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who caucuses with Democrats, and 10 Democratic lawmakers also voting “nay.”

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire said she couldn’t pledge her support for the bill as it “gives the President new authority to impose tariffs, even on our allies. I do not think tariffs, which are paid for by American businesses and consumers, will help Ukraine win this war.”

Similarly, a spokesperson for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia told TIME the lawmaker could simply not support the tariff powers included in the current version of the bill.

“Sen. Ossoff continues to support Ukraine’s valiant self-defense against intolerable Russian brutality and aggression,” the statement read. “He does not support the provisions of this bill that delegate massive new tariff authorities to a President who has demonstrated he will wield tariffs recklessly and destructively.”

President Donald Trump’s global tariff efforts, the majority of which were struck down by a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year, remain a contentious issue. Just last week, Trump announced a new round of tariffs on more than 80 countries.

Graham—a longtime supporter of Ukraine and one of the Senate's most outspoken foreign policy hawks—spent more than a year negotiating the legislation, which stands to impose tougher sanctions on Moscow and penalize countries that continue to buy Russian oil, gas, and other exports. Essentially, it's intended to cut revenues from the sale of ​Russia's energy for its war on Ukraine.

A key section of the bill states that “not later than 30 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the President shall, notwithstanding any other provision of law, increase the rate of duty for all goods, including oil, natural gas, liquefied natural gas, petroleum, petroleum products, petrochemical products, coal, and coal products, imported into the United States from the Russian Federation to a rate of up to 500 percent ad valorem.”

Regarding the President’s tariff authority, if the bill were to become law, it would allow Trump to place tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, among other penalties.

Graham announced during a visit to Kyiv, just shortly before his death, that he had secured the White House’s approval on his revised text.

The latest iteration also includes a last-minute addition of extended sanctions against Iran, at the request of Trump. Following Graham’s passing, and amid the resumption of the Iran war, Trump said on July 19: “Republicans should add Iran to the Russian Sanctions Bill. That’s what Lindsey wanted to do, and it was going to happen.”

The gathering of Senators and international leaders for Graham’s funeral service in Washington on Tuesday set the ideal stage for the bill to be discussed.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who had earlier sat down with Trump in the Oval Office, was hosted by the bill’s bipartisan leaders in the evening.

Democratic Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire joined Republican Senators Jim Risch of Idaho, Roger Wicker of Mississippi, and Katie Britt of Alabama in facilitating Zelensky meeting other supporters of the legislation and allowed him to address the Senate.

Before watching the bill advance inside the Senate chamber, Zelensky told reporters: “Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important and it's not only about money. It's also a big signal to Europe and a big signal to Ukraine, a big support of our people.”

An earlier version of the legislation drafted by Graham would have authorized the President to impose 500% tariffs on Russian products, as well as tariffs of up to 500% on countries that purchased Russian oil and gas.

Paul argued those provisions would "cause an economic calamity on a scale never before seen in" America.

But concerns remain regarding the tariff authority still afforded to Trump, should the legislation go all the way—meaning the bill’s chances of passing the Senate and the House of Representatives once it resumes at the end of the summer are not guaranteed.

Democratic Rep. Gregory W. Meeks of New York, ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has already raised "serious” concerns.

“This is not so much a sanctions bill as it is a massive backdoor authority for President Trump to impose more tariffs, including on our European allies, that hurt American families,” he said upon reviewing the text earlier this month. “The sanctions the bill does contain are entirely at Donald Trump’s discretion, and he has made clear repeatedly that he would rather waive sanctions on Russia than impose new ones.”

item.title: Is Farmers’ Market Produce Safer During the Cyclospora Outbreak?
item.description: Food-safety experts weigh in on where and how to shop for safer produce right now.
item.content:encoded:
As Cyclospora cases continue to mount across the U.S., shoppers from Kentucky to Michigan are flocking to local farmers’ markets in search of safer produce. But are farmers’ markets actually less risky than grocery stores when it comes to avoiding cyclosporiasis and other foodborne illnesses?

Some food-safety experts say farmers’ markets could be a safer bet, though that depends on where the produce actually comes from and the practices of the individual farmer. “If you are getting produce directly from the farmer who grew it, I would consider that lower risk,” says Kalmia Kniel, a professor of microbial food safety at the University of Delaware.

Other experts say produce from supermarkets isn't inherently more dangerous, and that consumers can take steps—both at the grocery store and the farmers’ market—to protect themselves from foodborne bugs.

Darin Detwiler, an associate teaching professor of food policy at Northeastern University and author of Food Safety: Past, Present, and Predictions, says he personally favors farmers’ markets because locally grown produce typically travels a shorter distance, passes through fewer processing and distribution steps, and can offer more transparency about where and how it was grown. 

But he says consumers shouldn’t assume that all produce sold at a farmers’ market is local. He says he always asks vendors which farm the produce comes from, how far away it was grown, and when it was harvested. Detwiler says he prefers if the produce is grown within about 30 miles and sold within two days of harvest.

Rodney E. Rohde, chair of the Medical Laboratory Science Program at Texas State University, says it makes sense that people perceive produce sold at farmers’ markets as being safer—but he says there is little scientific evidence to back that up. “The risk of contamination really depends on how it was grown, harvested, transported and stored, rather than where it is sold,” he says. 

In the case of Cyclospora, contamination can occur when human sewage gets into water used to irrigate fresh produce, says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute of Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University. That’s one reason locally grown produce isn’t automatically safer: A farm’s water and growing practices still matter most.

A smaller farm is also not necessarily better, says Don Schaffner, a food-science expert at Rutgers University. “Small farmers often do not have the resources that large operations” do, he says. 

Food-safety experts stress that people should continue to buy and consume produce—whether at the grocery store or the farmers’ market—despite Cyclospora fears. “Don’t quit eating fruits and vegetables,” Rohde says. But people can take precautions to limit their risk of Cyclospora and other foodborne pathogens.

Bill Marler, a food-safety lawyer, recommends buying intact heads of lettuce and whole fruits and vegetables over bagged, boxed, or pre-cut produce. Centralized chopping, washing, mixing, and packaging can spread contamination from a relatively small amount of produce across a much larger batch, he says. 

Experts also advise washing produce thoroughly under running water, scrubbing hard fruits and vegetables such as melons and cucumbers, and following other food-safety practices, such as keeping raw meat and vegetables separate when cooking. 

Cooking food to an internal temperature of at least 158°F can kill Cyclospora. Rohde says he has been cooking most of his veggies lately and has been washing produce “more vigorously than usual.”

item.title: Fauci Pleads the Fifth at Senate Hearing on COVID, Escalating Long-Running Clash With Republicans
item.description: The hearing escalates Fauci's long-running clash with Republicans as they seek to revisit the disputed origins of the coronavirus and the U.S. pandemic response.

media:group.media:description: Dr. Anthony Fauci, the longtime infectious disease expert who helped lead the federal government's response to the COVID pandemic, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday, refusing to answer questions at a Senate hearing that Republicans had hoped would expose him to potential perjury charges and discredit his handling of the nation's pandemic response.

item.content:encoded:
Dr. Anthony Fauci, the longtime infectious disease expert who helped lead the federal government's response to the COVID pandemic, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday, refusing to answer questions at a Senate hearing that Republicans had hoped would expose him to potential perjury charges and discredit his handling of the nation's pandemic response.

Appearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the panel's Republican chairman and one of Fauci's most persistent critics, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases declined to answer questions just minutes into the hearing, saying Paul had made clear his goal was to seek his prosecution.

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said in his opening statement. He accused Paul of having an "obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution" and said the Senator's release of his personal pandemic diary was intended to intimidate and embarrass him.

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect that I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress," Fauci said, "under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."

The hearing marked a dramatic moment in the yearslong political battle over the pandemic. Fauci, who advised seven presidents and became the nation's most recognizable public health official during COVID, has appeared before Congress hundreds of times over four decades;  Wednesday was the first time he invoked the Fifth Amendment.

The infectious disease expert has been a primary target of Republicans' continuing effort to revisit the government's response to the pandemic and the disputed origins of the coronavirus, issues that have remained central to conservative criticism of Fauci years after he left government service in 2022. Paul and other Republicans have long alleged that the National Institutes of Health funded so-called gain-of-function research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology that contributed to the pandemic, an accusation Fauci has consistently denied. Fauci has maintained that, under the government's definition of gain-of-function research, NIH did not fund such work related to the virus that caused COVID. Federal reviews have not reached a definitive conclusion about the virus's origin, and there is no evidence it was engineered and leaked from a laboratory.

Former President Joe Biden gave Fauci a preemptive pardon in the final hours of his Administration in an effort to protect him from politically motivated charges. But Paul, who has repeatedly accused Fauci of misleading Congress about federally funded virus research in China and the origins of COVID, argued the hearing was necessary regardless. "A pardon that protects a person from criminal prosecution doesn't rewrite history," the Kentucky Senator said in his opening statement. "It does not erase documents. It does not convert a misleading statement to a truthful one, and it does not prevent Congress from establishing what happened."

Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, Paul released roughly 1,100 pages from Fauci's pandemic-era diary, arguing the documents showed discrepancies between Fauci's private thinking and his public testimony. 

As Paul pressed ahead with questions despite Fauci's refusal to testify, the former health official responded each time with the same statement: "On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution."

At one point, Paul remarked, "Let the record record that the witness has refused to answer whether there's a folder in front of him based on his Fifth Amendment right."

The hearing also unfolded amid mounting pressure from Trump Administration officials to revisit Fauci's testimony under oath. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said earlier this week that Fauci could face perjury charges if he lied during the hearing despite Biden's preemptive pardon, arguing, "There are many things that (Fauci) said that we know are lies," and adding that "if he lies again, then he could be subject to perjury prosecution."

President Donald Trump likewise weighed in before the hearing, saying on Truth Social that Fauci "made too many bad calls" during the pandemic and asserting that he "didn't let (Fauci) shut the Country down." Trump has repeatedly criticized Fauci's recommendations on masks, shutdowns, and other public health measures.

Biden's pardon shielded Fauci from federal prosecution over actions and testimony connected to his government service during the pandemic. But Republicans have argued that any false statements made in new testimony could expose him to fresh legal jeopardy, a possibility Paul openly discussed before the hearing.

Asked this week about concerns that the hearing was designed to lure Fauci into committing perjury, Paul dismissed the criticism. "There's no risk to perjury if you tell the truth," he told reporters. "The only thing he can't do is lie again."

Democrats criticized the hearing as a partisan exercise. Senator Gary Peters of Michigan, the committee's top Democrat, argued the panel should be focusing on current national security threats rather than revisiting disputes over the pandemic. "Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today's hearing looks backwards," Peters said at the hearing. "Rather than building on that work to strengthen our preparedness against future disasters, we are instead relitigating the past."

item.title: How to Stop Being So Defensive During Arguments
item.description: You don’t need a better rebuttal. You need a reset.

media:content.media:credit: Photo-Illustration by TIME (Source Image: years/Getty Images)

item.content:encoded:
Here's a reliable way to tell that an argument has gone sideways: You started out discussing who was supposed to load the dishwasher, and you're now somewhere in the vicinity of a canceled dinner in 2019, your mother-in-law, or whether anyone in this household appreciates anyone else.

"It's like, ‘Wait, how did we get here?’" says Jessica Harrison, a couples counselor in Rhode Island. "That's a sign that somebody somewhere is being defensive."

It can be difficult to recognize when you’re being defensive, because it rarely feels that way. It feels like accuracy—like you’re finally setting the record straight. Meanwhile, the actual problem—the one somebody worked up the nerve to raise—never gets solved. It’s now buried underneath four brand-new ones. As Harrison puts it: “Who can manage and conclude five arguments in one conversation?”

The instinct to defend yourself isn’t a character flaw. It’s a protective reflex that can kick in when something threatens your sense of who you are. “We have the fight-or-flight response to protect ourselves from physical danger,” says Eli Kraiem, a clinical psychologist in New York who specializes in couples therapy. “But there’s also that same component to protecting our ego or our sense of self, which not everyone is as aware of.” In other words, a relatively ordinary complaint can feel like a verdict on who you are—especially when it comes from someone you care about. The alarm sounds, and suddenly you’re presenting Exhibit A for why you are, in fact, an excellent partner who does plenty around here, thank you very much.

That protective instinct isn’t always a bad thing. Sometimes you need to set a boundary or protect yourself, says Dr. Jeff Katzman, a psychiatrist at Silver Hill Hospital in New Canaan, Conn. But when defensiveness becomes your default response during ordinary disagreements, it can take a toll over months and years. Partners drift apart while ostensibly discussing chores. Friends stop bringing things up. “Whenever we become defensive, we start to become more certain about our perspective, and we go to battle in some way,” Katzman says. “The more defensive we become, the lonelier we become.” 

The goal isn’t to eliminate defensiveness entirely. It’s to recognize it sooner, respond more thoughtfully, and know how to repair the conversation when you slip up. Here’s what experts recommend.

Learn your body's tell

Defensiveness often starts in your body before you even utter a word. Reuven Rosen, a couples therapist in Columbia, Md., asks clients: “What happened in your body the moment your partner said that?”

The answers tend to be specific and physical. “There's going to be a knot in my throat, there's going to be maybe a tightness in my stomach, a tightness in my chest, maybe my heart's beating,” he says.

These sensations are easy to overlook, but they can serve as early warning signs that you’re about to interrupt, deny, or fire back. When you notice your heart racing or your chest tightening, pause and ask yourself why you’re having such a strong reaction. That brief check-in can give you a chance to choose what to say next—instead of automatically going on the defensive. 

Ask what you're trying to protect

Once you notice yourself becoming defensive, reflect on this: “What am I actually trying to protect?” It’s probably not the specific point you’re arguing about. More often, it’s something personal—your belief that you’re a good partner, a dependable friend, or a competent employee. 

“When we're being defensive, we're ultimately trying to protect something, whether it's a value, a moral, our character, or our confidence in being able to do something,” Harrison says.

Figuring out what feels threatened can quickly change the conversation. A request for more help around the house might come across like this: “You think I’m a bad partner.” But that’s not necessarily what the other person said—or meant. They might simply be asking you to take on more around the house.

Harrison suggests asking yourself: “Am I protecting my character or my values right now, or am I actually listening to what this person is telling me?”

Sometimes, you become defensive precisely because being a good partner—or friend or employee—matters so much to you. “It's a sign that they care so much that they're terrified of getting it wrong,” Harrison says.

Trade certainty for curiosity

Defensiveness has a way of making you feel absolutely certain: You’re right, they’re wrong, and if you could just explain yourself clearly enough, they would finally see it. But the harder you work to prove your point, the less attention you’re paying to theirs.

Katzman, who has spent decades in improvisational theater alongside his clinical work, suggests doing the opposite. “The way out is not to think faster,” he says. “It's really to become curious sooner.”

Improv offers a surprisingly useful model. Onstage, “blocking” means rejecting the premise your scene partner has introduced. If they announce that it’s raining and you insist that it isn’t, the scene has nowhere to go. “When we block each other, that's what defensiveness really does,” Katzman says. “I'm negating your reality, you're negating mine.”

The alternative is the improv principle of “yes, and.” In an argument, that might mean acknowledging the other person’s experience before adding your own perspective. Another improv rule applies, too: “Make your partner look good,” Katzman says.

That doesn’t mean agreeing with everything the other person says. It means remembering that you’re on the same team. “We're after understanding, not winning,” Katzman says. “The goal is to move from being certain to being curious.”

Look for the 2% truth

Even criticism that feels unfair, exaggerated, or badly timed often contains a sliver of truth. Kraiem calls it the “2% truth.” Finding that 2% can be difficult—especially when you’re busy cataloging the other 98% the person got wrong—but acknowledging it can quickly lower the temperature.

Before you point out everything the other person has misunderstood, acknowledge the small part they got right. Say, for example, your partner accuses you of never listening. Your instinct might be to list all the times you did listen. Instead, try saying: “You’re right that I was distracted when you told me about your meeting tonight.” You’re not agreeing that you never listen; you’re acknowledging the part of the complaint that’s true. That can make the other person more receptive to what you say next.

The challenge is resisting the urge to debate whether the criticism is technically accurate and focusing instead on the feelings behind it. “We focus more on the intellectual perspective,” Kraiem says, “as opposed to: How can I connect to this person and understand where they're coming from, even if it doesn't make 100% sense to me?”

Retire "never" and "always"

Certain words carry tiny invitations to fight. Two are especially potent: “never” and “always.”

"When you default to these absolute words like ‘never’ and ‘always,’ you invite defensiveness in the other person," Katzman says. "They're just going to come up and try to prove you wrong." Tell someone they never do the dishes, and you’ve handed them a debate they can win on a technicality: They did the dishes last Thursday. Now you’re arguing about Thursday. The real message—”I need more help,” or “I need you to see everything I'm doing”—never gets delivered.

The same goes for grievance-stacking. Adding a second grievance, then a third, then the thing from last month, doesn't strengthen the case; it simply creates more things for the other person to dispute. "Somebody winds up having to defend themselves on seven fronts," Katzman says, "instead of just staying with the one thing that you're trying to figure out."

Reflect back before you explain yourself

When someone tells you that you hurt them, your first instinct might be to explain what you meant—or why they misunderstood you. But to someone who has just made themselves vulnerable, that explanation can sound like an excuse. It can also leave them feeling even less heard.

Kraiem recommends starting by summarizing exactly what you heard the other person say, then checking that you understood correctly. Don’t repeat a few words and immediately pivot to your side. Instead, he suggests saying something like: “What I’m hearing is that after the ice cream spilled, I raised my voice and used words that hurt you, and that left you feeling alone. Am I getting that right?”

This approach can also keep you from getting sidetracked into an argument about who said exactly what. Kraiem recently watched a couple spend several minutes going back and forth—”You said this.” “No, I didn’t”—before he stopped them. “Let's focus on the feelings that were felt in the room when this conversation happened,” he told them.

Acknowledge the impact—even if you remember it differently 

When Rosen’s 10-year-old son told him that he had shushed him after he tripped on the stairs and cried out, Rosen immediately wanted to dispute that version of events: “That didn’t happen. That’s not how it went.”

Then he noticed a dropping sensation in his stomach. When he paid attention to it, Rosen realized what the complaint had stirred up: a fear of how his son viewed him. Rather than argue about exactly what had happened, Rosen focused on how the experience had affected his son. “I’m sorry that that happened,” he told the boy, even though he didn’t remember it that way.

You don’t have to agree that every detail happened exactly as the other person remembers it to acknowledge that the experience hurt them. And doing so doesn’t mean your intentions—or your version of events—don’t matter. It simply means they don’t have to come first. Once the other person feels heard, you can explain what you remember and what you meant.

Keep a repair line in your back pocket

Sometimes the best thing you can do in the middle of an argument is stop trying to defend yourself and ask to start over. Be especially careful with the word “but”: “I see why you feel that way, but…” Everything that follows will probably sound like a rebuttal—and erase the acknowledgment that came before it.

Kraiem suggests memorizing a few simple repair lines: “I can see why what I did landed that way.” “You're right—I see how I hurt you.” “Help me understand what I'm missing here.” His favorite, and the one he uses at home, is: “I'm sorry, can we try that again?”

These phrases won’t prevent every argument or mistake. “We're not going to eradicate fighting or mistakes that we make,” Kraiem says. What they can do is help you recover—to acknowledge that something came out wrong and give both of you a chance to handle the conversation differently.

Revisit the conversation afterward

You won’t always realize you’re being defensive while the argument is happening. Once you’ve calmed down, return to the conversation and explain what was behind your reaction. 

Harrison suggests wording it like this: “I'm sorry I responded that way. I realize you were just saying you wanted more help. What I was feeling was that you were telling me I was a bad partner—and I know that's not what you were saying. But I want so badly to be a good partner that I felt like I had to defend myself.”

Don’t rush back with an apology before you’ve figured out why you reacted so strongly. Otherwise, it can feel forced. “You're just kind of white-knuckling it,” Rosen says. Take some time to figure out what fear or insecurity was driving your reaction. Once you understand what you were defending, a sincere apology will probably come more naturally.

Ask what you want from the conversation

Katzman once found himself on the verge of arguing with a stranger at a restaurant. On a cold, windy night, he held the door open while his family walked inside. A woman seated near the entrance complained loudly about the draft. A waitress offered to move her, but she declined, saying she would be fine if “that man” would stop letting in the cold air. Then Katzman’s family was seated directly beside her—and she continued complaining.

Katzman could feel himself preparing to respond. Then the woman’s husband caught his eye and winked.

“He winked at me in a way that I felt like, oh, you see me,” Katzman says. “And I should see myself and wake up to the fact that I don't need to get into this argument.”

Before you continue an argument, ask yourself: “What am I hoping to accomplish here?” If you’re trying to understand the other person or resolve a problem, the conversation is probably worth having. If you simply want to prove that you’re right, stepping away might be the better choice.

Katzman still thinks about that wink when he feels himself getting pulled into an unnecessary argument. You can borrow it—or come up with your own cue that reminds you to pause and consider whether the conversation is worth having, he says. Sometimes the least defensive response is deciding not to argue at all.

item.title: Kentucky Governor to McConnell: Prove Fitness to Serve or ‘Resign’
item.description: Democrat Andy Beshear sent a letter to the Republican Senator who has been absent from his public duties and faces questions about his health status.

media:content.media:description: Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., makes his way to a vote in the U.S. Capitol on April 30, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Two photographs supplemented by personal statements from Sen. Mitch McConnell (R, Ky.), who has been absent from Congress since mid-June, have not quelled doubts about his health status. Now, Kentucky’s Democratic governor has demanded that the veteran GOP lawmaker prove his fitness for office or resign.

Gov. Andy Beshear sent a letter to McConnell on Monday, “under the assumption that he is capable of reading and responding verbally, and not incapacitated by means of consciousness or cognition,” following McConnell’s hospitalization on June 14. 

In the letter, Beshear called on the 84-year-old to “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.” Beshear also sent a similarly worded letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune and urged him to “fully investigate” McConnell’s condition, report to the public if the ailing Senator did not voluntarily show his ability to serve, and assess if Senate proceedings were warranted.

In most states, governors appoint new senators to fill vacant U.S. Senate seats, but Kentucky’s state law requires a special election to be held instead.

The letter went public as McConnell’s office released a statement in which the Senator said he could not attend an upcoming event in the state. Beshear doubled down in his own letter on what McConnell has missed since disappearing from public view—including casting crucial Senate votes. “Important events are happening in our country right now during your absence,” Beshear said.

It was only weeks after June 14 that McConnell first disclosed that he was hospitalized due to a fall. The lack of details has fueled rumors of his potential disability and even death, among critics, and has also become a subject of mockery.

McConnell has previously attributed his prolonged silence about his fall and subsequent hospitalization to vulnerabilities surrounding aging and privacy. But the Kentucky Governor said that while he understands the Senator’s concerns, he noted that as a public official, McConnell was expected to “willingly abdicate much of your personal privacy.”

“It’s not like we are asking a lot,” Beshear told CNN Tuesday. “We’re asking the bare minimum.”

Asked about the letter, Thune told NBC News on Tuesday that the issue was between McConnell and Kentuckians: “I’m not sure what [Beshear’s] prerogatives are in that case. But that’s where the issue should be resolved.”

The Democratic Governor has been widely viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 presidential election.

Concerns about gerontocracy

McConnell’s prolonged absence, as well as the sudden death of his colleague, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R, S.C.), at 71, have brought renewed attention to what many say is a growing problem in U.S. politics: the main players are getting too old to play the game.

Data from the Pew Research Center show that the median age of Senators at the start of the current U.S. Congress was 64.7 years. The House leans slightly younger, with a median age of 57.5 years. Americans’ median age, meanwhile, is 39.4 years.

But aging in public office has been particularly spotlighted in the executive.

Donald Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, who was the oldest President to leave office at 82 years and 2 months old, had his cognitive health questioned during the 2024 election cycle. Biden later dropped out of the race following a disastrous debate performance.

Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and became the oldest U.S. President to take the oath of office. At 80, he has faced increasing scrutiny over his physical condition and mental acuity, and his Administration has conducted several health assessments in an attempt to dismiss concerns. And despite his age, Trump has even teased running for an unconstitutional third presidential term.
